narration.text: In Gull Harbor, it rains two hundred days a year. Drizzle was ready for every one of them.
He was ready for rain. He was not ready for this.
At 10:42 on a Tuesday morning, his coffee cup started to shiver. Then the floor moved.
Every instinct told him to run for the doorway. That's an old myth. In a modern house, a doorway is no stronger than any other part of the wall, and it's right where things fall on you.
So he did the thing that works.
Under the table. One hand gripping a leg. One arm over his head.
Mags from next door was already under there with him. She'd come over for coffee. She was staying for this.
Ten seconds. Twenty. A minute. Small earthquakes end fast. This one didn't.
The shaking lasted four minutes. Long enough to know exactly what it was. The Cascadia fault, seven hundred miles of it, had finally let go.
Then the lights went out.
When the shaking stopped, the kitchen was full of broken glass and one very loud question. Now what?
Gull Harbor sits right on the coast. And on the coast, a quake that long means one thing. The ocean is coming.
She was right. On the coast, the shaking is the warning. There may never be a siren.
Drizzle grabbed his laptop. His photo album. A plant. Then he put them all down.
The go-bag by the door had everything that mattered. Water. A flashlight. A radio. Medicine. A warm layer. Packed months ago, for exactly this. It took three seconds to grab.
Outside, Gull Harbor looked wrong. Windows shattered. Power lines down. The street cracked open like a dropped plate.
And down at the harbor, something stranger. The water was leaving.
Boats sat in the mud. Fish flopped on the sand. A few people walked out to look. That's the deadliest mistake on the coast. When the sea pulls back, it comes back bigger.
Cars were already jammed on Harbor Way. Horns blaring. Going nowhere.
Cracked roads. Fallen lines. Gridlock. Feet don't get stuck in traffic. Drizzle and Mags walked uphill.
The evacuation trail was steep, muddy, and exactly where the signs said it would be.
Point four miles to the hilltop. On a normal day, ten minutes. With aftershocks, longer.
Halfway up, Mags' knees gave out. Drizzle gave her his shoulder. They kept moving.
Official word, finally. But by then, everyone who'd listened to the shaking was already climbing.
Drizzle looked back. A gray line stretched across the whole horizon. It wasn't a cloud.
Twenty-two minutes after the shaking stopped, the first wave hit Gull Harbor. It took the dock. The ferry. Then Main Street.
Drizzle wanted to stop and watch. Mags didn't let him.
Tsunamis come in waves, for hours. The first one is often not the biggest. You don't go back down until officials say it's safe.
The hilltop was cold, crowded, and above the water. That was all that mattered.
Town volunteers had a tarp up and a check-in table running. The school had walked every kid up the hill. They'd practiced.
Drizzle counted what he'd done right.
One. Drop, cover, hold on. Two. On the coast, the shaking is your warning. Walk uphill, now. Three. Grab the go-bag, not your stuff.
And four. He'd brought snacks.
Then the radio spoke again.
The only road out was gone. The whole coast had been hit at once. Help would come. Just not today. Maybe not this week.
Below them, the water was still rising. Night was coming. And somewhere down in the dark, a light flickered on where no one should be.
